title: Predict how by-value parameters and ref, out, or in affect caller storage

rubric.point: Explains that the by-value parameter receives a copy of the object reference, so changing Reading mutates the object shared by current and saved.
Explains that assigning a new Meter to the by-value parameter changes only the parameter's reference, leaving both caller variables pointing to the object whose Reading is 12.
Explains that ref aliases current's storage, so assigning the new Meter replaces current's reference and makes current.Reading equal 0.
Explains that saved remains a separate variable pointing to the original object, whose Reading is 12.

questions.model:
By value, `item` holds a copy of the reference stored in `current`. All three variables initially refer to the same object, so `item.Reading = 12` changes the object visible through both `current` and `saved`. Assigning a new object to `item` then changes only that local parameter. Both caller variables still see `12`.

With `ref`, `item` aliases the variable `current`. The first assignment still changes the original object's reading to `12`. The second assignment replaces the reference stored in `current`, so `current.Reading` becomes `0`. `saved` is a separate variable and still references the original object, so `saved.Reading` remains `12`.

rubric.point: Explains that out must be assigned on every normal return path, including a return of false.
Gives a correction that assigns limit before the false return and explains that the assignment writes into the caller's variable.
Explains that in provides readonly access through the parameter, so limit = 30 is forbidden and should be removed.
Explains that out supplies an assigned value on normal return, whereas in reads an existing value and therefore requires an initialized argument.
